chapter: Guitar, John Collins and Ellington on the radio
title: First hearing Duke Ellington on the radio and Cootie Williams growl
summary: At 13 or 14 he heard Ellington's orchestra broadcast with Cootie Williams's growl solos, which at first shocked him.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Now, how do you mean the Ellington situation?
When I started listening to the Duke Ellington Orchestra, you know?
And how old were you when you started listening to the Duke Ellington Orchestra?

Oh, boy, wait a minute. The first time I heard him on the radio. He was working at exclusive clubs there, and he would come on maybe 15 minutes, about dinner time. That's the way they were doing it in those days on radio. I guess I was about 13, 14. You know, 13 or 14. And he shocked me. I don't know, I guess he meant to shock everybody. He had Cootie Williams playing and around Chicago in those days we had oh, Jan Garber, and everybody listening to Guy Lombardo. And about dinner time Duke would have Cootie Williams to play a growl solo.
And we just didn't -- you know, everybody was eating steaks or something, you know, whatever, and here comes this trumpet on the air, playing growl solos, you know.

And I said, 'Gee whiz, what the heck is that,' you know? And I didn't know whether I liked it before, but then it grew on me. I didn't know whether I liked it or not, because it was so new to me, you know?
As I was talking to Jerome Richardson one day, he said he didn't get into Duke until later, because see he loved Jimmy Lunceford, as I did.
But Ellington, he finally captured everybody, you know?
